fields.meaning: At least, at the very least
examples: If you're going to be late, at least give us a call.
When meeting someone for the first time, let's at least greet them properly.
Even if you're busy, you can at least read a message, right?
Before the exam, at least memorize the vocabulary.
Even if you forget your wallet, at least have your fare money on you.
You should at least apologize to him.
fields.explain:
Often used together with せめて to strengthen the nuance of a "minimum."
What comes before くらいは is something obvious/basic, so use it with subordinates/acquaintances to avoid sounding rude.
Suitable in recommendations/rules:参加する くらいは 義務だ。

• Emphasizes the minimum acceptable level: "at least…".
• Speaker's attitude: often accompanies a reminder, a mild reproach, a minimum request, or a suggestion.
• The target before くらいは is something "easy to do/basic," or a small amount.
fields.notes:
• After くらいは there is usually a clause expressing an expectation/request (～しなさい／～してほしい／～べきだ…).
• In business emails, use it indirectly to be polite: ご連絡くらいはいただけますと幸いです。
• It can be used with a negative to emphasize the minimum: それくらいは難しくない（at least that isn't difficult）。
mistakes: Confusing it with くらい (degree): くらいは requires the particle は to create the meaning "at least."
Using it with a request that is too strong in a polite context can sound rude; add ください／いただけますか.
Do not use it for something beyond the "minimum"; if you are asking for a lot, use べき/必要がある instead of くらいは.

examples: Tomorrow, for sure
This year, I'm going to really give it my all.

examples: This restaurant's food is certainly tasty, but the portions are small.
I can speak Japanese well enough, but I'm weak with technical terms.
It is convenient, sure, but the fees are high.
I will go, but today might not be possible.
It is necessary, yes, but not right now.
fields.explain:
You must repeat the same word/same stem to create the emphasis of concession.
"が/けど" can be swapped; "けれども" is more formal.
Usually used in the general present; the tense can change if the context allows, but keep the two clauses parallel.
The nuance is gently polite and avoids an absolute assertion.

• Partially acknowledges something in the first clause, but gives a limitation/exception/different point in the second clause: "It is … all right, but …".
• The nuance emphasizes reservation, not complete denial.
• The second clause usually states a reason/condition that changes the final evaluation.
fields.notes:
• Emphatic form: ～のは～のだが also exists, but it is a different structure.
• You can insert an adverb between the two repetitions to fine-tune the nuance: 少し高いことは高いが…
• In spoken language, が can be omitted, ending the sentence and continuing the idea in the next sentence.
meaning_vi: 「確かに～だが、その事実はあまり重要ではなくて、…。」
It is certainly true that ~, but that fact is not very important, so …
examples: 1. 彼からの手紙は読んだことは読んだんですが、意味がよくわかりませんでした。
I did read his letter, but I didn't really understand what it meant。
2. わたしは泳げることは泳げますが、長い距離はだめなんです。
I can swim, but I can't swim long distances。
3. この本は高いことは高いが、写真が多くて楽しめそうです。
This book is certainly expensive, but it has lots of photos, so it looks like it will be enjoyable。
4. 子どもを育てるのは大変なことは大変だが、成長が楽しみで大変さを忘れる。
Raising children is certainly hard, but the joy of watching them grow makes you forget the hardship。
mistakes: Not repeating the same word: ×おいしいことは美味だが… → it must be the same stem: おいしいことはおいしいが…
Confusing it with "Vることはある" (something happens occasionally). That is a pattern with a completely different meaning.
Wrong combination with na-adjectives: ×便利だことは便利だが → correct: 便利なことは便利だが。
Overusing it with nouns in ordinary conversation is unnatural; prefer verbs/adjectives.

fields.meaning: A negative question; an expression with a meaning like "ですね"
examples: You don't look well, do you?
You don't look well. Did something go wrong?
"Huh? Where did I put my glasses?" "They were right there a minute ago, weren't they?"
That skirt is cute! It really suits you.
fields.notes: A casual way of saying 「Ｖ－ようではないか」.

examples: Thanks to the discount, I didn't have to buy the expensive bag.
Because I went to the hospital early, I managed to avoid surgery.
The rain stopped, so I didn't have to take a taxi.
When I explained it to my boss, I got away without being scolded.
I had shared the materials in advance, so I didn't need to give a long explanation at the meeting.
fields.explain:
Has a nuance of relief and luck; to keep it neutral, add the adverb なんとか/うまく.
Used with a result that is positively contrary to expectation: なんとか間に合って謝ら ずにすんだ。
In natural spoken language: ～ないで済んだ; formal/written: ～ずに済んだ.
Used with で済む/で済まない to talk about degree:罰金で済んだ（got off with just a fine）.

～ずにすんだ expresses "did not have to do …; managed to avoid …", usually with a nuance of relief or luck at not needing to carry out an action that was planned or that should have been done.
• Presupposition: the speaker thinks X would normally have to be done, but in reality it was not.
• Often used with costly, troublesome or painful things: 手術, 追加料金, 叱られる, 謝る, 行列する.
• Can be used in the present/potential: ずにすむ（現在）, ずにすんだ（過去）.
• It is not necessarily a good result, but most of the time it carries a feeling of "luckily."
fields.notes:
• The classical negative "ずに" = "ないで". With する → せずに; 来る → 来ずに（こずに）.
• In reports, you can add a reason: ～のおかげで／～ために + ずにすんだ.
• Negating the nuance of luck: ～ずにすまず（could not avoid） is rare and written language.
mistakes: Wrong sound change of する: it must be せずにすんだ, not "しずにすんだ".
Confusing the meaning "didn't do" with "didn't need to do": ～ずにすんだ includes the idea of "avoided."
JLPT: a trap is choosing ～なくてもいい instead of ～ずにすんだ; if there is a past result "managed to avoid" → choose ～ずにすんだ.
Combining it with something positive that does not fit the context: "ご飯を食べずにすんだ" usually implies something negative for health; consider the context.

fields.connection: Vます(drop ます) + そうにない
examples: At this pace, it doesn't look like we'll make the deadline.
The rain doesn't look like it will stop tonight.
He's stuck in traffic, so he's unlikely to arrive on time.
This problem doesn't look like something children could understand.
Prices don't look like they'll come down for the time being.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to say "unlikely to happen" while staying polite and avoiding absolute negation.
Often used in reports/forecasts:回復しそうにない,改善しそうにない.
Combine with どうも/この様子では to emphasize that it is based on observation.

• Expresses the prediction "unlikely to/doesn't look like it will …; low possibility."
• Based on the current situation or objective conditions, not on subjective will.
• The nuance is relatively objective and softer than a direct negative; more polite than "V-るのは無理だ".
fields.notes:
• In risk reports, use ～そうにない to avoid flatly asserting "no," leaving room for a change of plan.
• Combined with expressions of duration: しばらく／当面／当分＋V-そうにない strengthens the nuance of "not anytime soon."
• Impersonal subjects fit well: 天気・相場・交通・業績・回復.
meaning_vi: Hardly likely to…, very unlikely to…
explain: Emphasizes a stronger degree of pessimism than ～そうにない; often used with adverbs: とても／どう見ても／この調子では.
Used when you want to suggest changing plans: ～そうもないから、Aに切り替えよう.
Suitable in both spoken and written language; not overly formal.
examples: 1. この量では、今日中に終わりそうもない。
With this amount of work, there's no way it will be done today.
2. バスは来そうもないから、歩いたほうがいい。
The bus doesn't look like it's coming, so we'd better walk.
3. 彼はあの件について謝りそうもない。
He doesn't seem at all likely to apologize about that matter.
4. 予算が足りないので、新機種の導入はできそうもない。
The budget is insufficient, so introducing the new model seems impossible.
5. この天気だと、明日の試合は開催されそうもない。
With this weather, tomorrow's game seems unlikely to be held.
comparison: Pattern | Degree of "impossible" | Nuance | Short example
～そうにない | Low possibility | Mild, objective | 帰（かえ）れそうにない。
～そうもない | Very low/hardly any | "も" adds emphasis, somewhat pessimistic | 帰（かえ）れそうもない。
～ようがない | Absolutely impossible | There is no way to do it | 連絡（れんらく）の取（と）りようがない。
～っこない（spoken language） | No way | Casual, strong negation | 今（いま）からじゃ間（ま）に合（あ）いっこない。
common_mistakes: • Confusing the degree with ～そうにない: when choosing an answer in the exam, look for "も" to spot the emphasis.
• Using this form with adjectives → incorrect; switch to the pattern for adjectives.
• Combining it with the potential form can be unnatural: prefer the plain V + そうもない (間に合いそうもない).
meaning_vi: doesn't seem at all able to～
explain: The possibility of an action or event being carried out or happening is very low.
examples: 1. 最近仕事がすごく忙しくて、同窓会に行けそうにないよ。
Work has been really busy lately, so I don't think I can make it to the class reunion.
2. できそうもないことを、できると言ってしまって後悔している。
I regret saying I could do something that I can't possibly do.
mistakes: Using the form ～そうにない with adjectives → incorrect; use ～くなさそうだ／ではなさそうだ.
Confusing the degree with ～そうもない: the JLPT tests the nuance "mild vs very difficult."
Mixing it up with ～なさそうだ of ある; do not say ×ありそうにない.

examples: This restaurant is cheap. On top of that, the service is good too.
It's raining. On top of that, it has even started thundering.
He has a wealth of experience. Moreover, he is highly respected.
My fever won't go down. On top of that, my cough has gotten worse.
The explanations are easy to understand. Moreover, there are lots of examples, which helps a lot.
fields.explain:
Placed at the beginning of the added clause; usually followed by a comma after その上、 to mark a pause.
Tone: used in presentations, written language and evaluations; increases persuasiveness by listing reasons.
Combines well with だけでなく, ばかりか, さらに to build a chain of arguments.

• Adds information in the same direction: one more reason/strength/weakness to reinforce the argument.
• The nuance is somewhat more formal than それに; close to しかも in degree of emphasis but more neutral.
• Works at the sentence level: it stands at the start of the second clause, linking to the preceding clause; その上 is followed by a comma or a sentence break.
• Can be used for both positive and negative things: その上、遅刻してきた (negative), その上、親切だ (positive).
fields.notes:
• "その上" can also link a negative clause to add weight: 時間がない。その上、予算もない。
• In essays, the structure 第一に…、第二に…、その上… is used to add points.
• Avoid overusing it consecutively; limit it to 1–2 times per paragraph to avoid repetition.
meaning_vi: Moreover, in addition… (adds something in the same direction) explain: Suitable in essays, reports and advertisements: strengthens a point with evidence/additions in the same direction.
The two sentences should be logically related in the same direction; avoid combining opposite directions (good → bad).
The subjects can differ, but the topics should be closely related to avoid sounding disjointed.
Add a comma after そのうえ to make the rhythm of the sentence clear. ⏐ examples: 1. この店は安い。そのうえ、品質もいい。
This shop is cheap. On top of that, the quality is good too.
2. 彼は親切だ。そのうえ、仕事も早い。
He is kind. In addition, he works fast too.
3. 昨日は寒かった。そのうえ、風も強かった。
Yesterday was cold. Moreover, the wind was strong too.
4. 彼女は遅刻した。そのうえ、宿題も出していない。
She was late. On top of that, she hasn't handed in her homework either.
5. この薬はよく効く。そのうえ、副作用が少ない。
This medicine works well. Moreover, it has few side effects. ⏐ comparison: Pattern | Nuance | Difference | Short example
そのうえ | moreover (formal) | Reinforces in the same direction | 安（やす）い。 そのうえ、便利（べんり）。
それに | besides (neutral) | More colloquial, lighter | 安（やす）い。 それに 便利（べ explain: Usually used when you want to add one more characteristic of a thing, matter or person.
Usually used with an implication of praise, raising it even higher. ⏐ examples: 1. この店の料理はおいしい。その上値段も安い。
The food at this restaurant is delicious. On top of that, the prices are low too
2. 彼は、頭がいい。その上スポーツも何でもできる。
He is smart. On top of that, he can do any sport too
mistakes: Confusing it with しかも: しかも has strong emphasis and a sense of surprise; その上 is more neutral.
Using it in a very casual sentence sounds bookish; in conversation, それに is usually chosen.
JLPT: trap questions ask you to choose a conjunction by nuance; for a formal/logical style → その上; for exclamation/surprise → しかも.

examples: Strict regulations were introduced. As a result, emissions fell sharply.
I couldn't prepare enough. As a result, I failed the exam.
We continued the investigation. As a result, we were able to identify the cause.
Those results will be shared at the next meeting.
We adopted a new strategy. As a result, profits recovered.
fields.explain:
Formal; suited to academic writing and business reports.
Usually placed at the beginning of a sentence with a comma: "その結果、～"。
Used as a noun meaning "that result": attaches to は/が/を…
Can be used with "として" to emphasize the consequential relationship: その結果として～。

• "As a result/Therefore" emphasizes the cause-and-effect relationship and the final outcome after a process.
• Usually used in written language, reports and theses; the nuance is more formal than それで/だから.
• The premise (cause, process) must be clear in the preceding sentence/paragraph so that "その結果" has an accurate reference.
• Can be used for positive, negative or neutral results.
fields.notes:
• In a long paragraph, use "この/その/前述の結果" to keep the reference clear.
• "～の結果" (the result of N/V): 交渉の結果／調査した結果、～（a very common pattern）.
• In argumentation, combine it with "一方で／しかし／つまり" to create a tight logical flow. explain: Used when something that happened in the past is the reason leading to the consequence of the next event. Used as a connective linking two sentences. ⏐ examples: 1. 父は、人の何倍も努力した。その結果、仕事で成功した。
My father worked many times harder than other people. As a result, he succeeded in his career
2. 3ヶ月ダイエットを続けた。その結果、5キロやせた。
I stayed on a diet for 3 months. As a result, I lost 5 kilos
mistakes: No clear premise before "その結果" → the reader doesn't know "the result of what."
Confusing it with "そのために" (purpose) in reading comprehension questions; pay attention to the context of result vs purpose.
Repeating "その結果" too often in the same paragraph → alternate with そのため／したがって／結果として.
Using "結果は" when you actually mean "経過/要因は" → identify correctly what you need to state.

examples: Bread, and a coffee too, please.
Please tell me your address and phone number.
Oh, and also, tomorrow's meeting is canceled.
This color is nice. And the price is reasonable too.
That and this are two different matters.
fields.explain:
Casual and natural in everyday conversation.
Used at the beginning of a sentence to add information that just came to mind, gently shifting the topic.
In formal documents, replace it with そして/または/および/ならびに depending on the context.

• A colloquial conjunction meaning "and/besides," used to add the next item or piece of information.
• Conversational nuance, softer than そして; can be used as a light shift, "oh, and also…."
• When listing nouns, "それと" separates relatively independent items; it does not emphasize temporal order like それから.
fields.notes:
• In a long list, "A、B、それとC" highlights the last item, like "and also C."
• It can carry the nuance of "just remembering" a secondary piece of information in conversation.
• When legal/technical precision is needed, avoid それと and use および/並びに.
mistakes: Using それと to express cause and result: ×雨。それと中止になった → use それで/そのため.
Using it in formal documents such as reports/regulations → inappropriate; replace with および/ならびに/また.
Confusing it with それから (temporal order) and それに (addition with a positive evaluation); the JLPT often tests this nuance.

fields.meaning:
「～が原因だ。 ・～が原因で…という結果になる。」 …には普通希望・意向・相手への働きかけなどの文は来ない。少し硬い言い方。
~ is the cause./ ~ is the cause that leads to the result …
Sentences expressing a desire, an intention, or an appeal to the listener to do something are not used in the … part. It is a somewhat formal expression.
fields.connection: V/A plain form + ためだ・ため(に)… / Nの + ため(に)（cause）
examples: The many mistakes in the report were probably because it wasn't checked carefully.
Because there is no doctor in this village, people have to go all the way to the neighboring town when they are sick.
Owing to a business trip, I will be absent from tomorrow's meeting.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: Expresses a cause. 「～から」、「（のは）～ためだ」 has the same meaning as 「（・・・のは）～からだ」
examples: 1. ①　雪が降ったため
Because it snowed
2. ②　雪が降ったため（に）、電車が遅れた。
Because it snowed, the train was late.
3. ③　会議が延期されたのは、社長の体調が悪いためだ。
The meeting was postponed because the company president is not feeling well.

fields.meaning: Expresses a result that is the opposite of what one would generally expect.
examples: When I took it, it actually…
I was in a hurry, so I took a taxi, but it actually ended up taking longer.
I skipped things like lunch to lose weight, but I actually ended up gaining weight.

fields.meaning: The casual way of saying 「～てはいけません」
examples: You mustn't buy it
If you buy such expensive clothes, you'll run out of money.
You have to eat a proper breakfast, you know.

fields.meaning:
「～するのがいいですよ。」 助言や忠告の気持ちで相手にある行為を軽く進めるときに使う。④のように、その行為をしないことを非難する言い方にもある。
It would be good to do ~.
Used when gently suggesting, encouraging or advising the listener to do something.
As in example ④, it is also a way of criticizing the listener for not doing it.
examples: If you're worried about your health, why don't you get a medical checkup once?
You look tired. Why don't you take a little rest?
You're getting a lot of spam? Then why not change your address?
You're the one at fault. Why don't you at least apologize?
fields.notes: An idiomatic expression of suggestion or recommendation. It is often used in the form 「Ｖ－てみたらどうか」. It is almost synonymous with 「てはどうか」, but 「たらどうか」 is more typical of spoken language. In casual speech, 「たらどうなの／どうかしら（女性）」「たらどうなんだ（男性）」「たらどう（男女）」 are used, and in polite speech, 「たらいかがですか／いかかでしょうか」 and so on. ③④ are used in situations where the listener does not readily follow the speaker's advice or recommendation, and carry the speaker's irritation. ⑥ has the latter part omitted and is pronounced with rising intonation.（２１３）
